claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing discrete W particles or interconnected W ligaments in a Cu matrix.
Conventional high-temperature processing of the W–Cu composite produces phase separation.
Conventional high-temperature processing of the W–Cu composite produces interfacial voids.
Rapid quenching immediately after high-temperature processing will suppress phase separation in W–Cu.
Rapid quenching will inhibit interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
Rapid quenching will produce a metastable, homogeneous W–Cu interfacial microstructure with reduced diffusional gradients.
Reduced diffusional gradients and a homogeneous interface will minimize sites for void nucleation.
Rapid quenching kinetically limits atomic diffusion at W–Cu interfaces.
Interfacial phase separation and coarsening lead to interfacial void formation in W–Cu.
Freezing in a uniform interfacial microstructure preserves continuous thermal-conduction pathways during subsequent high-heat-flux and irradiation exposure.
Rapid-quenched W–Cu will have higher thermal conductivity than conventionally cooled W–Cu under identical service-like tests.
Rapid-quenched W–Cu will retain more stable thermal conductivity during heat-transfer and irradiation testing.
Rapid-quenched W–Cu will have a lower interfacial void density than conventionally cooled controls.
Phase-separated, void-containing untreated W–Cu has lower thermal conductivity under operational heat-transfer and irradiation conditions.
The intervention is applicable to W–Cu composites processed by high-temperature sintering or annealing.
The applicable service boundary includes high thermal gradients and moderate-to-high irradiation doses relevant to plasma-facing-component joints.
The intervention may fail when the quench rate is too low to arrest diffusional processes.
Alloying additions can dominate the composite's microstructural evolution and negate the proposed quench effect.
